title: Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, existentialism, analytic philosophy
note: Kierkegaard defended passionate, personal faith against Hegel's system. Nietzsche announced the death of God and called for a revaluation of values. Existentialists stressed freedom and responsibility. Analytic philosophers, from Frege and Russell to Wittgenstein, turned to logic and language, while thinkers like Plantinga brought those tools to the philosophy of religion.

read.title: The single individual and the limits of language
text: In the nineteenth century, Hegel built a vast system in which history unfolds as reason coming to know itself. Søren Kierkegaard protested that no system can live a human life. Truth that matters most must be appropriated by a particular person in passion and decision. In Fear and Trembling he pictures Abraham, who trusts God's promise even when commanded to give up Isaac, as a knight of faith whose relation to God cannot be reduced to universal ethical rules.

Friedrich Nietzsche drew the opposite conclusion about religion. Declaring that God is dead, he meant that belief in God had lost its cultural authority, and he warned that the morality built on it would collapse too. He hoped for new values that affirm life.

Twentieth-century existentialists such as Sartre held that humans have no fixed nature given in advance; we define ourselves by our choices and are responsible for them. Others, like Gabriel Marcel, developed existential themes within Christian faith.
Meanwhile analytic philosophers turned to logic and language. Wittgenstein first argued that sentences picture facts, then later that meaning lies in the use of words within shared forms of life.

q.q: What was Kierkegaard's complaint about Hegel's system?
o: No system can live a human life

q.q: What did Nietzsche mean by 'God is dead'?
o: Belief in God had lost its cultural authority
God had been proven not to exist by science

q.q: How did the later Wittgenstein locate meaning?
o: In the use of words in shared life
